indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Yes, a certified copy from a marriage register can be used as evidence of marriage. Under section 80 of the Christian Marriage Act, 1872 ([1]), such a certified copy is admissible in evidence without requiring further proof of the register or entry.

question: When may the court order an alleged adulterer to pay case costs?
expected_section_title: Power to order adulterer to pay costs
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Under The Divorce Act, 1869 (section 35), a court may order an alleged adulterer (as a co-respondent) to pay case costs if adultery is established in a petition by the husband. However, this does not apply if the respondent was living apart and leading a prostitute’s life, or if the co-respondent had no reason to believe the respondent was married. Similarly, The Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936 (section 33) allows courts to order the adulterer to pay costs in divorce suits based on adultery, provided the plaintiff has made the adulterer a co-defendant (unless the court excuses this).

retrieved_context.section_title: Power to order adulterer to pay costs
retrieved_context.text: 35. Power to order adulterer to pay costs. Whenever in any petition presented by a husband, the alleged adulterer has been made a co-respondent, and the adultery has been established, the Court may order the co-respondent to pay the whole or any part of the cost of the proceedings : Provided that the co-respondent shall not be ordered to pay the petitioner's cost — (1) if the respondent was, at the time of the adultery, living apart from her husband and leading the life of a prostitute, or (2) if the co-respondent had not, at the time of the adultery, reason to believe the respondent to be a married woman.

In every such suit for divorce on the ground of adultery, the plaintiff shall, unless the Court shall otherwise order, make the person with whom the adultery is alleged to have been committed a co-defendant, and in any such suit by the husband the Court may order the adulterer to pay the whole or any part of the costs of the proceedings

Any husband may, either in a petition for dissolution of marriage or for judicial separation, or in a petition to the ¹[Court of Civil Judge] limited to such object only, claim damages from any person on the ground of his having committed adultery with the wife of such petitioner. Such petition shall be served on the alleged adulterer and the wife unless the Court dispenses with such service, or directs some other service to be substituted. The damages to be recoverd on any such petition shall be ascertained by the said Court, although the respondents or either of them may not appear. After the decision has been given, the Court may direct in what manner such damages shall be paid or applied.

answer:
Property disposition rules can be extended to the Khoja community by the Provincial Government issuing a notification in the Official Gazette, as outlined in section 5 of the Hindu Disposition of Property Act, 1916. This notification would substitute the word 'Khojas' for 'Hindus' wherever applicable, thereby applying the Act's provisions to the Khoja community in the specified area.

retrieved_context.text: 27. Conditional transfer to one person coupled with transfer to another on failure of prior disposition.— Where, on a transfer of property, an interest therein is created in favour of one person, and by the same transaction an ulterior disposition of the same interest is made in favour of another, if the prior disposition under the transfer shall fail, the ulterior disposition shall take effect upon the failure of the prior disposition, although the failure may not have occurred in the manner contemplated by the transferor. But, where the intention of the parties to the transaction is that the ulterior disposition shall take effect only in the event of the prior disposition failing in a particular manner, the ulterior disposition shall not take effect unless the prior disposition fails in that manner. *Illustrations*

question: When is a husband liable for his wife’s breach of trust as a trustee or executrix?
expected_section_title: Extent of husband's liability for wife's breach of trust or devastation
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Under [1], a husband is not liable for his wife's breach of trust or devastation unless he actively acts or intermeddles in the trust or administration. This means his liability is conditional on his own involvement in the matter. question: When is adultery treated as condoned in a marriage dispute?

indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Adultery is treated as condoned in a marriage dispute under the Divorce Act, 1869 only if conjugal co-habitation has been resumed or continued after the adultery [1]. This means that the petitioner must have restarted or maintained marital living arrangements with the spouse who committed adultery for it to be considered condoned.

question: What punishment can a minister face for solemnizing a minor’s marriage without required consent?
expected_section_title: Solemnizing without notice or within fourteen days after notice, marriage with minor
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Under the Christian Marriage Act, 1872, a minister who solemnizes a minor’s marriage without required parental/guardian consent may face imprisonment for up to three years (section 70) or, if additional conditions like failing to send notice copies apply, up to five years (section 71).

answer:
A divorce or annulment petition under Pakistani law must explicitly state that there is no collusion or connivance between the petitioner and the other party to the marriage, as required by section 47 of The Divorce Act, 1869 [1]. This declaration must be verified by the petitioner or a competent person, as per legal requirements for verifying plaints [1]. Examples in the passages show this is phrased as: 'no collusion or connivance exists between me and my said wife...' [4] and similar statements [5].

retrieved_context.text: 26. Decree of separation obtained during absence of husband or wife may be reversed. Any husband or wife, upon the application of whose wife or husband, as the case may be, a decree of judicial separation bas been pronounced, may, at any time thereafter, present a petition to the Court by which the decree was pronounced, praying for a reversal of such decree, on the ground that it was obtained in his or her absence, and that there was reasonable excuse for the alleged desertion, where desertion was the ground of such decree. Under [1], a husband must name the alleged adulterer as a co-respondent in a divorce petition unless the court excuses him on specific grounds, such as the respondent being a prostitute with unknown partners, the adulterer's identity being unknown despite efforts, or the adulterer being dead. question: Are a married woman’s own wages treated as her separate property?

indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Yes, under section 4 of the Married Women's Property Act, 1874, a married woman’s wages and earnings from her own employment, occupation, or trade (not through her husband) are deemed her separate property. This includes savings and investments from such earnings, and she alone is responsible for their management.

Under section 14 of the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936, knowingly making a false marriage certificate can result in simple imprisonment for up to three months, a fine of up to 100 rupees, or both. answer: پاکستانی قانون کے تحت، شادی کا جھوٹا سرٹیفکیٹ بنانے یا اس پر دستخط کرنے پر سزا ہو سکتی ہے جو اس میں شامل مخصوص عمل پر منحصر ہے۔ پارسی شادیوں کے لیے، جرمانہ تین ماہ کی سادہ قید یا 100 روپے تک کا جرمانہ، یا دونوں ([1]) ہے۔ عیسائی شادیوں کے لیے، جرمانے میں تین سال تک کی قید اور جرمانہ ([2]) شامل ہو سکتا ہے۔ مزید برآں، اگر یہ عمل جعل سازی کا حامل ہے، تو پاکستان پینل کوڈ (پی پی سی) کی دفعہ 466 کے تحت جرمانے لاگو ہو سکتے ہیں ([1])۔-- بازیافت شدہ قوانین صرف جزوی طور پر آپ کے سوال سے میل کھا سکتے ہیں۔ یہ قانونی مشورہ نہیں ہے۔ حوالہ کردہ ذرائع یا اہل وکیل کے خلاف ہر چیز کی تصدیق کریں۔

question: Can a marriage certificate be issued after two months have passed since it was granted?
expected_section_title: Persons authorized to solemnize marriage(other than Clergy of Churches of Enland, Scotland or Rome);
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
No, a marriage certificate cannot be issued after two months have passed since it was granted. According to section 26 [2], if a marriage is not solemnized within two months of the certificate being issued, the certificate becomes void. Additionally, section 71 [5] and section 72 [1] explicitly state that issuing a certificate after this period (or without proper authorization) is an offence under the Pakistan Penal Code.

question: When can a licensed person grant a marriage certificate?
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
A licensed person can grant a marriage certificate when the conditions in section 60 of the Christian Marriage Act, 1872 are fulfilled, upon application by either party and payment of a fee of four annas. The licensed person must be authorized under section 9 of the Act by the Provincial Government to grant certificates between Native Christians.

question: What inheritance issue is addressed for certain Hindu heirs with disabilities?
expected_act_name: THE HINDU INHERITANCE (REMOVAL OF DISABILITIES) ACT, 1928
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
The Hindu Inheritance (Removal of Disabilities) Act, 1928 addresses the exclusion of certain Hindu heirs with disabilities from inheritance or joint-family property rights. Specifically, Section 2 of the Act states that no person governed by Hindu law (except those who are or have been from birth a lunatic or idiot) can be excluded from inheritance or property rights due to disease, deformity, or physical/mental defects [2]. This amendment removes existing Hindu law rules that previously allowed such exclusions [1].

question: Can a testamentary guardian sell or mortgage a ward’s immovable property despite a restriction?
indexing_note: used_source_indexes are 1-based positions into retrieved_chunks, matching finalize_rag_ask (same order as chunks_to_sources / prompt [1]..[n]).
answer:
Yes, a testamentary guardian can sell or mortgage a ward’s immovable property despite a restriction if the Court, after declaring them guardian, permits it by an order in writing. Otherwise, their powers are subject to any restrictions imposed by the instrument appointing them [1].

retrieved_context.section_title: Powers of testamentary guardian
retrieved_context.text: 28. Powers of testamentary guardian. Where a guardian has been appointed by will or other instrument, his power to mortgage or charge, or transfer by sale, gift, exchange or otherwise, immoveable property belonging to his ward is subject to any restriction which may be imposed by the instrument, unless he has under this Act been declared guardian and the Court which made the declaration permits him by an order in writing, notwithstanding the restriction, to dispose of any immoveable property specified in the order in a manner permitted by the order.

retrieved_context.section_title: Limitation of powers of guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court
retrieved_context.text: 29. Limitation of powers of guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court. Where a person other than a Collector, or than a guardian appointed by will or other instrument, has been appointed or declared by the Court to be guardian of the property of a ward, he shall not, without the previous permission of the Court,— (a) mortgage or charge, or transfer by sale, gift, exchange or otherwise, any part of the immoveable property of his ward, or (b) lease any part of that property for a term exceeding five years or for any term extending more than one year beyond the date on which the ward will cease to be a minor.

retrieved_context.section_title: Variation of powers of guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court
retrieved_context.text: 32. Variation of powers of guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court. Where a guardian of the property of a ward has been appointed or declared by the Court and such guardian is not the Collector, the Court may, from time to time, by order, define, restrict or extend his powers with respect to the property of the ward in such manner and to such extent as it may consider to be for the advantage of the ward and consistent with the law to which the ward is subject.

retrieved_context.text: 34. Obligations on guardian of property appointed or declared by the Court. Where a guardian of the property of the ward has been appointed or declared by the Court and such guardian is not the Collector, he shall,— (a) if so required by the Court, give a bond, as nearly as may be in the prescribed form, to the Judge of the Court to ensure for the benefit of the Judge for the time being, with or without sureties, as may be prescribed, engaging duly to account for what he may receive in respect of the property of the ward; (b) if so required by the Court, deliver to the Court, within six months from the date of his appointment or declaration by the Court or within such other time as the Court directs, a statement of the immovable property belonging to the ward, of the money and other moveable property which he has received on behalf of the ward up to the date of delivering the statement, and of the debts due on that date to or from the ward;

retrieved_context.section_title: Fiduciary relation of guardian to ward
retrieved_context.text: 20. Fiduciary relation of guardian to ward.—(1) A guardian stands in a fiduciary relation to his ward, and, save as provided by the will or other instrument, if any, by which he was appointed, or by this Act, he must not make any profit out of his office. (2) The fiduciary relation of a guardian to his ward extends to and affects purchases by the guardian of the property of the ward, and by the ward of the property of the guardian, immediately or soon after the ward has ceased to be a minor, and generally all transactions between them while the influence of the guardian still lasts or is recent.

retrieved_context.section_title: Duties of guardian of property
retrieved_context.text: 27. Duties of guardian of property. A guardian of the property of a ward is bound to deal therewith as carefully as a man of ordinary prudence would deal with it if it were his own, and, subject to the provisions of this Chapter, he may do all acts which are reasonable and proper for the realisation, protection or benefit of the property.
